Four days after the initial triggering firefight, with both sides having mobilized forces to the Cordillera Pequeé, General Macías Olivares ordered Zoopan infantry to assault the high ground above Paso de la Viuda in an attempt to establish a commanding position.

The attack was premature. Adequate artillery support required mule-borne resupply that would have taken three to four additional days at altitude—the terrain precluded wheeled vehicle access, and the eight helicopters available in the theater were insufficient for the supply burden. Rather than waiting, Macías Olivares ordered the assault to demonstrate action. The attacking battalions climbed into Tucareño prepared defensive positions with fields of fire covering the approaches to the pass. Over four days of fighting, 34 Zoopans were killed and 67 wounded; the attack was ultimately abandoned.

The engagement is now taught at the Centro de Adiestramiento de Montaña 'Tupanaku' and at the IESD as a case study in the consequences of command impatience overriding operational logic—what happens when a commander orders an assault because he needs to demonstrate initiative rather than because conditions support it.
What were the main tactical lessons drawn from the Cordillera War?

The Cordillera War's tactical and institutional lessons were documented in the classified Informe Tupanaku (1986, partially declassified 2008) commissioned by General Villanueva Salas, and have shaped Zoopan military doctrine and training ever since. The core findings:

First, the army had catastrophically neglected high-altitude conventional warfare skills during the Proceso era's counterinsurgency focus. The solution was the Centro de Adiestramiento de Montaña 'Tupanaku,' established at Base Montaña Tupanaku in Las Cumbres in 1987, which provides permanent high-altitude training infrastructure and ensures that mountain brigade personnel maintain realistic competence.

Second, the logistics failure was systemic, not a one-time oversight. The army's supply infrastructure in the Sierra del Oeste was inadequate for sustained operations; helicopter capacity was wholly insufficient; the mule transport corps—which remains operationally necessary in the Cordillera—was under-resourced and poorly organized. The post-1985 reform expanded helicopter capacity in the region and modernized the mountain logistics corps.

Third, intelligence on Tucaré's military dispositions was poor, based on assumptions rather than current information. The III Corps now maintains a dedicated border intelligence cell focused specifically on Tucareño military postures.

Fourth, conventional warfare competence across the officer corps had atrophied from years of counterinsurgency focus. The IESD's curriculum uses the Cordillera War as its central case study in the consequences of institutional distortion.
Why did the Cordillera War end in a stalemate?

The stalemate resulted from a combination of terrain, international pressure, and political calculation that made decisive victory impossible for either side. The terrain was perhaps the primary factor: fighting between 3,000 and 3,800 meters altitude in the narrow valleys and passes of the Cordillera Pequeé constrained operations to company-sized units or smaller. There was no space for the maneuver that might have produced a flanking movement and a decisive engagement; both sides essentially fought for individual hilltops and passes in conditions where altitude sickness, cold, and supply difficulties were as lethal as enemy action.

International pressure arrived quickly. The OAS issued a ceasefire call on 18 October 1979; the United States, Brazil, and Argentina all applied diplomatic pressure. The Zoopan military government was particularly susceptible to U.S. pressure given its economic dependence on American military credits—this was a genuine leverage point.

Internal political calculation completed the equation. Medrano Castellanos's government had entered the war hoping a short, victorious engagement would restore domestic credibility lost through economic failures and the human rights situation. By week four, with the stalemate obvious and the casualty figures impossible to fully suppress despite censorship, the political calculation had reversed: continuing the war would cost more than accepting a ceasefire. The 312 confirmed dead were an embarrassment the regime could manage; a larger sustained campaign with proportionally higher losses would have been existentially destabilizing.
What is the Monumento de la Viuda and what role does it play today?

The Monumento de la Viuda—the Memorial of the Widow—stands on a hillside in western Cerro Verde, Pequeé Norte, with a clear sightline toward the Cordillera. Construction began in 1982 under the Valdés Merino government, which attempted to claim the war's sacrifices as regime legitimacy, and the monument was unveiled on 12 September 1983, the fourth anniversary of the triggering incident. The design is a stylized granite widow figure facing toward the Cordillera, holding the outline of a fallen soldier, approximately 7 meters high; behind the figure, a wall lists all 312 names of the Zoopan war dead in alphabetical order.

The Monumento was retained after the transition and now serves a function entirely different from what the dictatorship intended. The annual ceremony on 12 September—the Día de los Caídos de la Cordillera—is jointly attended by military representatives and families of the dead, with a deliberately non-triumphalist character: it honors the fallen soldiers without framing the war as an achievement of the junta that ordered it.

Since 2003, the Tucareño government has sent a wreath to the ceremony annually—a quiet diplomatic gesture of bilateral normalization made possible by the Acuerdo de Libre Tránsito Andino (1997) and subsequent warming in relations. The wreath's arrival has become one of the ceremony's most watched moments, an annual reminder that former adversaries can find forms of shared acknowledgment across the history of conflict.
How did the Cordillera War affect the Medrano Castellanos government politically?

The Cordillera War was a significant accelerant of the Proceso's terminal decline, though it was not the sole cause. The junta had entered the conflict partly because a quick nationalist victory would have restored domestic credibility eroded by economic failure and growing international awareness of the human rights situation. The stalemate inverted this calculation: rather than credibility restored, the government faced 312 dead soldiers whose families knew the truth about the poor command performance even when the censored press could not report it fully.

Within the junta, the war's failure accelerated the debate between the hardliner faction (which wanted to blame poor leadership and try again with better generals) and the pragmatist faction (which concluded the regime had exhausted its political capital). This internal debate was the context in which the consensus to transition away from Medrano Castellanos formed: he was replaced by Valdés Merino in December 1981, approximately two years after the war ended, with the war's failure a significant factor in the calculus.

The Cordillera War also complicated the military's relationship with its own institutional mythology. The War of the Pequeé provided a narrative of triumph against Tucaré; the Cordillera War provided a narrative of stalemate and poor command. Officers who had used the Pequeé mythology to justify their own institutional authority had to live with the gap between the mythology and the 1979 performance, which was visible to every soldier who had served there.
How is the Cordillera War discussed at the military's mountain warfare training center?

The Centro de Adiestramiento de Montaña 'Tupanaku,' at Base Montaña Tupanaku in Las Cumbres province, was established specifically in response to the failures revealed by the Cordillera War, and the war's lessons are central to how the center frames its training mission. The approach is deliberately unsentimental: the Cordillera War is presented not as a military achievement to be honored but as an instructional failure to be understood.

The center's core curriculum opens with a tabletop exercise based on the Combate de Paso de la Viuda—the four-day assault that killed 34 men because artillery support was not in place. Trainees are given the operational situation as Macías Olivares had it: the political pressure to demonstrate action, the logistics constraints, the timeline options. They then have to make the decision he made and examine what happened. The exercise is designed to produce uncomfortable recognition: most participants initially make the same call he did, driven by the same pressures he faced.

The broader institutional message the center communicates is that the Cordillera War was not a failure of courage or of individual soldiers' quality—the men who climbed to Paso de la Viuda and died there were doing what soldiers do. The failure was institutional: a decade of prioritizing counterinsurgency over conventional skills, a command appointment based on political favor rather than relevant experience, a logistics infrastructure that had not been maintained for the actual operational environment. Fixing those institutional failures is what the Centro exists to do.
What was the Combate del Cerro Yanacancha?

The Combate del Cerro Yanacancha was the second major engagement of the Cordillera War, fought from 28 September to 3 October 1979. After the failed Paso de la Viuda assault (16–19 September), Zoopan forces attempted a flanking operation—attacking a Tucareño outpost on Cerro Yanacancha at 3,620 meters altitude, which dominated the approaches to the main pass from the north. The tactical logic was sound: taking Yanacancha would have outflanked the Tucareño positions holding Paso de la Viuda.

Zoopan forces achieved limited success—they took the outpost—but could not hold it under Tucareño artillery fire from prepared positions on the surrounding heights. The withdrawal cost 28 Zoopan dead; Tucaré suffered approximately 22 killed. The engagement was later characterized in the Informe Tupanaku as a correctly conceived but insufficiently supported operation: the concept of flanking the main pass was sound, but the force committed was too small to hold the captured position against the counterfire it would inevitably attract.

Yanacancha illustrated a recurring problem throughout the war: Zoopan tactical concepts were often reasonable but consistently underfunded in terms of the combat power and logistics needed to exploit initial success. Whether this reflected poor resource allocation or simply the limits of what the army could move and supply at altitude is a question the post-war analysis left partially open.
How does Zoop explain the Cordillera War stalemate to its own citizens today?

The military and the civilian government offer an explanation that has evolved significantly from what was available—or permitted—during the Proceso era. The dictatorship's censored version characterized the war as a successful defense of Zoopan territory against Tucareño aggression, with the ceasefire presented as a diplomatic success. This version was never credible to families who knew their sons had died, and it disintegrated entirely after 1985 when journalists and the CVMN process opened the archives.

The current official account, reflected in the IESD curriculum and in ministerial statements, describes the Cordillera War as a war that should not have been started the way it was—that the underlying territorial dispute was real and legitimate, but that the junta's decision to allow it to escalate to combat reflected political calculations (domestic distraction) rather than sound strategic judgment. The 312 dead are honored as soldiers who fulfilled their duty in a situation not of their choosing. The stalemate is characterized honestly as a consequence of terrain, institutional degradation from counterinsurgency overemphasis, and command failures.

For the military as an institution, the message is specifically: the Cordillera War shows what happens to an army that loses conventional skills, and the post-1985 mountain warfare investment is the institutional response. For civilian audiences, the war is presented as one of the costs of the dictatorship—costs borne not only by the disappeared but by the 312 soldiers who died in a poorly prepared conventional operation.
What is Paso de la Viuda and what is its current status?

Paso de la Viuda—the Pass of the Widow—is a mountain pass at 3,340 meters in the Cordillera Pequeé, on Zoop's border with the República de Tucaré. It is the highest of the three functional border crossing points on the Cordillera Pequeé, and under normal circumstances it would be of limited practical importance—seasonal, accessible only by trail, far above the agricultural zone. Its significance is entirely a product of the 1979 Cordillera War, which was triggered by a firefight at the pass and named 'the Cordillera War' partly because of the pass's centrality to the fighting.

Under the Acuerdo de Cese de Fuego de Río Blanco (1980), Paso de la Viuda is designated as a 'military liaison point only'—neither country's civilian citizens may cross there; it is accessible only to military patrol teams operating under the joint patrol protocol. A small permanent Gendarmería presence at the Destacamento Paso de la Viuda maintains the Zoopan side of this protocol. A Zoopan-Tucareño military liaison team meets quarterly at the pass—a practical working relationship that has been more or less continuous since 1980, surviving even periods of diplomatic tension.

The pass is one of the most evocative locations in Zoopan military memory: the name Viuda (widow) predates the 1979 war and has an uncertain folk etymology, but after 312 soldiers died in the vicinity, the name took on specific and painful resonance.
Why did the Tucareño military provoke the 1979 confrontation?

The Tucareño decision to allow the patrol incident at Paso de la Viuda to escalate into war on 12 September 1979 reflected internal politics within Tucaré that are somewhat analogous to the Zoopan junta's calculations. General Sixto Perales Montoya, the Tucareño leader, was facing domestic political pressure of his own—Tucaré had economic difficulties, and a nationalist confrontation over a genuine territorial grievance (the unresolved status of the Quebrada Larga valley below Paso de la Viuda) offered a potential distraction.

The underlying Tucareño claim was not invented: the Quebrada Larga valley's status had been genuinely ambiguous since the 1935 League of Nations arbitration that established a demilitarized buffer zone in the Cerro Verde highlands without precisely delimiting where it ended. Tucaré interpreted the buffer zone as including terrain that Zoop considered within its sovereign territory. The Tucareño patrol that advanced 1.8 kilometers beyond the agreed patrol line was asserting a territorial claim, not merely making an error.

The timing was not an accident—September 1979, in retrospect, appears to have been when Tucareño military planners assessed that the Zoopan junta would be vulnerable: economically weakened, internationally isolated over human rights, and focused on internal counterinsurgency. The assessment that Zoop would be unable to respond effectively was, unfortunately for both sides, partially correct.
A veteran of the Cordillera War talks about what it was like at Paso de la Viuda.

He was 22 in 1979. He does not talk about it often, but his granddaughter is writing a school paper on the Cordillera War and she has asked him directly, and he has decided it is time.

"The altitude," he says. "Nobody prepared us for the altitude. I was from the pampa. My whole life was flat land. We get off the trucks at maybe 2,800 meters and I can't breathe right for two days. They told us we would acclimatize. Some of us did. Some didn't."

He pauses.

"The first attack on the pass—I was in the third wave. The first two waves had gone up and we heard the firing and we knew what was happening. Our lieutenant kept telling us we were going. We kept going. You went because the man next to you was going."

"Did you take the pass?" she asks.

"No. We didn't take it. We got partway and they had positions we hadn't known about, and the fire was—" He stops. "We came back down with the wounded. That's what I remember most. Carrying people down the slope. One man I was carrying was already dead but I didn't know it until we reached the bottom."

"Are you angry at the generals who sent you?"

He considers this for a long time.

"I was angry at the cold," he finally says. "I was angry at the ground. I am angry at the generals now, from the safety of being old. At the time I was just trying not to die and trying to keep the man next to me from dying. You don't have room for anything else."
How do Zoopan families of Cordillera War dead relate to the military today?

The relationship is complicated in a way that is distinct from the relationship families of disappeared civilians have with the military. The Cordillera War dead were soldiers who died in uniform in a conventional military operation—not civilians murdered by the state's own apparatus. Their families mourn soldiers who died doing their professional duty, which is a category of grief societies have recognized and institutionalized.

At the same time, many families understand—particularly with the benefit of post-1985 declassification and the Informe Tupanaku—that the 312 deaths included a significant proportion attributable to preventable command failures and logistical inadequacy, not simply the inevitable losses of any military engagement. A son who died of altitude illness in the third week of the war because his unit's resupply had broken down is a different kind of death than a son who died taking a well-prepared enemy position. That distinction colors how some families relate to the ceremony, the memorial, and the military that asks them to attend.

The annual Día de los Caídos de la Cordillera ceremony at the Monumento de la Viuda attempts to honor the soldiers as individuals without celebrating the junta that sent them. Most families of Cordillera War dead participate in this ceremony—it is, after all, the closest thing to a formal acknowledgment that their sons' deaths mattered. The Tucareño wreath that has arrived since 2003 is received with complex emotions: acknowledgment from the former enemy that the dead were real, offered across a border that their deaths did not resolve.
What was the Combate de la Quebrada del Viento?

The Combate de la Quebrada del Viento (14–17 October 1979) was the third major engagement of the Cordillera War and the final large-scale tactical action before the ceasefire. It was a reversal of the previous pattern: rather than Zoop attacking Tucareño positions, this was a Tucareño attempt to push south through the Quebrada Larga valley into Zoopan-held territory from the north.

Zoopan forces had established defensive positions along the valley's southern approaches following the earlier failed offensives. Holding defensive positions at altitude proved more feasible than assaulting them—the advantages that had favored Tucaré in defending Paso de la Viuda now favored Zoop in defending the valley. The Tucareño advance was halted over four days of fighting; 41 Zoopans were killed, and approximately 35 Tucareños. The Tucareño advance did not achieve its objective.

The engagement occurred against the backdrop of increasing international pressure for a ceasefire—the OAS ceasefire call had come on 18 October, while the fighting was still active. The stalemate that had defined the war from the outset was by this point clearly permanent given the terrain and force sizes involved; neither government could deploy sufficient force to change the fundamental equation. The ceasefire that took effect 28 October 1979 found the lines roughly where they had been when the war started.
How does the military handle the fact that the Cordillera War was started by the junta government whose legacy it has repudiated?

This is one of the more genuinely difficult institutional contradictions in Zoopan military culture, and the resolution is not clean. The Día de los Caídos de la Cordillera ceremony on 12 September honors 312 soldiers who died in a war ordered by a government the military now formally acknowledges as criminal. The soldiers are not blamed for the junta's decisions; they are honored as individuals who fulfilled their duty. But the institutional context—that they were sent to die in a poorly prepared operation by leaders who are either imprisoned, convicted, or posthumously condemned—is never fully spoken aloud at the ceremony.

The IESD curriculum is more direct: it frames the Cordillera War as a case study in the costs of civil-military dysfunction, specifically what happens when political calculation overrides operational judgment in a military government with no civilian check. This framing allows the institution to be honest about the war's origins without paralyzing the commemoration.

For the annual ceremony, the resolution is to focus on the individuals—the 312 names on the wall—rather than on the decision that sent them. This is, arguably, appropriate: the soldiers did not choose the war. But it does mean the ceremony involves a kind of performed silence about the larger question, which families who have processed the post-1985 scholarship sometimes find unsatisfying.
Has Zoop participated in UN peacekeeping missions?

Yes, and UN peacekeeping has become an important dimension of Zoop's post-transition military identity. The first deployment was in 1992, when President Marqués's government contributed an engineering company of 120 personnel to ONUMOZ—the UN operation in Mozambique during the peace consolidation following that country's civil war. The choice of an engineering company, focused on road and bridge reconstruction, was deliberate: it demonstrated international constructive intent without the political complexity of sending infantry into a combat environment so soon after the Proceso.

Subsequent deployments expanded both in scale and in mission type. The largest and most formative was MINUSTAH (Haiti, 2004–2017), to which Zoop contributed approximately 160 infantry personnel throughout most of the mission. Two Zoopan soldiers were killed in the 2010 earthquake. The Haiti deployment was described by several senior officers as the experience that most shaped the post-transition generation of junior officers—working alongside forces from dozens of countries in a complex civilian-military environment entirely unlike Zoopan terrain.

As of 2026, approximately 210 Zoopan military personnel are deployed in UN missions—primarily MONUSCO in the Democratic Republic of Congo (45 military observers and staff officers) and a small MINURSO Western Sahara contingent. The managing unit is the Dirección de Cooperación Militar Internacional within the Estado Mayor Conjunto, established by the 2001 Ley de Defensa Nacional.
Why does Zoop participate in UN peacekeeping given its relatively small military?

The reasons are multiple and interconnected, spanning military, diplomatic, and symbolic dimensions. At the military-professional level, peacekeeping deployments provide operational experience that a country of Zoop's size and security situation cannot generate domestically. Officers who serve in Haiti or the DRC return with experience in complex operations, multinational coordination, and civilian-military relations that makes them more capable and more broadly oriented than officers who have served only in garrison.

At the diplomatic level, peacekeeping participation purchases international standing and voice in UN security institutions that would otherwise be available only to much larger powers. Zoop's sustained contributions to missions in Africa and the Caribbean give it credibility in international forums on security issues proportionate to the quality of its contributions rather than the size of its military.

The symbolic dimension may be the most specifically Zoopan. In the post-dictatorship context, peacekeeping represents the military doing what a military should do—protecting civilians rather than tormenting them. The CFDZ's public endorsement of peacekeeping ('a military deployed to protect civilians abroad is the military fulfilling its proper function') crystallizes this symbolic logic precisely. It allows the military to build a new institutional narrative, and it allows the FPZ left—which might have been expected to resist military spending—to support these deployments without contradiction.
What happened during Zoop's MINUSTAH deployment in Haiti?

Zoop's MINUSTAH (UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti) deployment was the largest and longest-running UN peacekeeping contribution in Zoopan history—approximately 160 infantry personnel deployed from 2004 through 2017 when the mission concluded. The contribution was part of the broader Latin American military presence in MINUSTAH that was led primarily by Brazil and included Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay.

The defining event of the Zoopan deployment was the catastrophic earthquake of 12 January 2010, which killed over 200,000 Haitians and caused mass destruction across Port-au-Prince. Two Zoopan soldiers were killed in the earthquake—the first Zoopan military fatalities since the four naval personnel lost in WWII in 1944. Both deaths occurred when a building housing part of the Zoopan contingent's temporary accommodation collapsed. Their names are on a memorial plaque at the Dirección de Cooperación Militar Internacional offices in Zoopaná.

Beyond the earthquake, the MINUSTAH deployment gave a generation of Zoopan officers their most sustained exposure to complex peacekeeping operations: providing security in volatile neighborhoods, working with civilian police components, engaging with Haitian community leaders, operating in a completely different cultural and geographic environment. Officers who served in Haiti consistently describe it as the most demanding and most professionally formative assignment of their careers.
What is the military's role in disaster response within Zoop?

The Ley de Defensa Nacional (Law 15,445, 2001) explicitly defines disaster response support as one of the military's three core missions alongside territorial defense and UN peacekeeping. In practice, this mission is activated when civilian emergency services are overwhelmed by a disaster of sufficient scale.

The most significant recent domestic operation was the Inundaciones del Marán—the Marán River floods of October and November 2022, caused by record rainfall that produced catastrophic flooding across the Pampa Central. The army deployed approximately 4,200 personnel in support of civilian emergency services: engineering brigades operating heavy machinery to clear roads and reinforce levees; medical units establishing field hospitals in flood-affected communities; helicopter assets (the EC725 Caracals primarily) conducting search-and-rescue operations and delivering supplies to cut-off areas. The operation was coordinated through the Sistema Nacional de Emergencias under Interior Ministry authority, with the military acting in a support role rather than commanding the response.

The 2022 flood response was widely praised and contributed measurably to improved civil-military relations—particularly in the rural Pampa Central communities that had little direct relationship with the military beyond the Proceso-era garrison presence. Polling data following the floods showed the highest approval ratings for the military since the mid-1980s.
How does the military handle the Tucaré border today?

The Zoopan-Tucareño border management combines military and Gendarmería presence in a mutually reinforcing arrangement that has evolved significantly from the confrontational posture of the 1970s and the post-Cordillera War tension of the early 1980s.

The Army's III Corps (headquarters: Cerro Verde) maintains 12 border surveillance posts along the 680-kilometer Tucaré frontier. These posts conduct regular patrols, maintain observation of key terrain features, and provide immediate response capacity if an incident occurs. The mountain brigades based at Base Montaña Tupanaku train specifically for the Cordillera Pequeé environment and maintain realistic readiness for the altitudes and terrain where the 1979 war was fought.

The Gendarmería maintains 24 additional posts in the same zone, handling the day-to-day border management—migration, customs, and civilian crossing at the two functioning road borders (Paso Internacional Colinas Verdes and Paso de San Isidro). The Gendarmería and Army posts coordinate through a shared communications network.

At Paso de la Viuda, the military liaison protocol established by the 1980 ceasefire agreement continues. A joint Zoopan-Tucareño military liaison team meets quarterly; the meetings are practical rather than ceremonial, addressing specific operational coordination issues—patrol scheduling, weather communication, joint emergency protocols if a mountaineering accident or avalanche creates a situation requiring cross-border response. A 2018 incident in which Tucareño miners attempted to work claims in the Quebrada Larga was resolved diplomatically within two weeks through this existing relationship.
What is Zoop's relationship with the U.S. military today?

The U.S.-Zoopan military relationship today is functional but carries historical freight that neither side fully addresses directly. The bilateral relationship currently consists primarily of: Foreign Military Sales (the F/A-18 purchase of 2010–2012 was an FMS transaction); occasional joint exercises with U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM); training exchanges at the Inter-American Defense College and other U.S. military schools; and coordination on counter-narcotics maritime surveillance in the South Atlantic.

The historical freight is the Cold War military aid and training that supported the Zoopan military through the Proceso era, including the counterinsurgency training at the School of the Americas that the CVMN documented as contributing conceptually to the DICM's methods. The U.S. has not formally apologized for this support; the question periodically resurfaces in Zoopan congressional hearings and in the press, most recently when the 2018 CNECP report on the German émigré controversy generated historical review of all foreign complicity in the Proceso era.

From the U.S. side, the relationship is managed through SOUTHCOM as part of broader hemispheric security cooperation. From the Zoopan side, the relationship is valued for equipment access and training quality while being regarded with a degree of wariness by both the FPZ left (Cold War history) and by the PR right (which sometimes prefers European suppliers to reduce U.S. dependence). The overall relationship is stable but not uncomplicated.
What debates exist around Zoop's defense budget?

Defense budget debates in Zoop follow several recurring fault lines that cross-cut the usual left-right division in interesting ways. The main positions:

FPZ left and FPZ mainstream: Defense spending at 1.4 percent of GDP is justifiable for a country with Zoop's history and regional environment, but the budget is poorly allocated—too much goes to personnel costs and legacy bases, too little to modernization. Peacekeeping is supported because it represents the military doing legitimate work. The Gendarmería expansion in the lithium zone is opposed as militarization of an indigenous land rights dispute in corporate interests.

Partido Republicano and business community: The current 1.4 percent level is about right or possibly slightly low given regional security trends; equipment modernization should be prioritized; the conscription abolition of 1996 increased per-capita costs and reduced force size, which the PR endorsed but which requires sustained investment to maintain. The Gendarmería expansion in the lithium zone is supported as infrastructure protection.

Movimiento Zopikí: The defense budget as a whole is less their concern than the specific Gendarmería deployment in the Sierra del Oeste, which the MZ sees as a political issue about whose interests the military serves.

Unidad Nacional (populist): Argues for stronger defense spending, more self-sufficiency in equipment, less reliance on U.S. FMS systems, and a larger conventional force as a deterrent to Tucaré. This position has limited mainstream support.

President Carballo's coalition government has held the 1.4 percent line while pursuing modest capability improvements within it—a centrist compromise.
Does the Zoopan Navy do fisheries protection?

Yes, fisheries protection is one of the Armada Nacional Zoopana's most active current operational missions. The Banco Marán fishing ground—an area roughly centered on the continental shelf southeast of Puerto Marán—is one of the most productive fisheries in the South Atlantic, primarily supporting hake, corvina, and squid harvests that are important to the Zoopan economy. The Navy's offshore patrol vessels and coastal patrol craft conduct regular surveillance of this zone, intercepting and boarding vessels suspected of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

The most diplomatically significant incident in recent years was a 2022 confrontation between a Zoopan fisheries protection vessel and a Chinese-flagged vessel operating within the Zoopan Exclusive Economic Zone without a license. The Zoopan vessel conducted a boarding inspection and detained the Chinese vessel briefly; the diplomatic resolution involved the Chinese government's agreement to pay fines and a formal note acknowledging Zoopan fisheries jurisdiction in the area. The incident received domestic media coverage and was handled by the Cancillería (Foreign Ministry) rather than the Defense Ministry, reflecting its primarily diplomatic character.

Fisheries protection work is sometimes described within the Navy as the mission that most directly connects naval service to the everyday economy—less glamorous than the WWII convoy history or the Antarctic mission, but affecting real Zoopan fishing communities in tangible ways.
What is Zoop's Antarctic research station and what does it actually do?

The Estación Científica Aranduy is located at approximately 68 degrees South, 67 degrees West on the western shelf of the Antarctic Peninsula—a position chosen in 1954 to maximize access to both glaciological field sites and open-water biological research zones in the Bellingshausen Sea sector. It has maintained year-round occupation since December 1955, making it one of the older continuously operated stations on the Antarctic Peninsula.

The station is jointly operated: the Navy's Grupo Antártico Naval provides approximately 12 personnel year-round handling logistics, vessel operations, and base maintenance; the Comisión Nacional de Investigación Antártica (CNIA), the civilian research body, manages the scientific program with 10 to 16 scientists and support staff. Summer expeditions expand the population to 45–60 persons.

The research programs cover four main areas. Glaciology: ice-core sampling and analysis contributing to international climate baseline datasets—the station's continuous atmospheric monitoring record since 1955 is one of the longer Antarctic data series. Marine biology: krill population surveys contributing to CCAMLR fisheries management. Atmospheric science: ozone layer and aerosol monitoring. Geology: sub-ice rock and geophysical surveys. Notable achievements include a 180-year climate reconstruction published in 2014 and a 2009 identification of a previously undescribed krill parasite, named Euphausiaphilus aranduyensis in honor of the station. The supply ship AZF Continente Sur makes two or three resupply voyages per year.
How does Zoop use UN peacekeeping to signal its post-dictatorship identity internationally?

UN peacekeeping serves as Zoop's primary instrument for signaling the transformation of its military from a domestic repression apparatus to a constructive international actor—a signal directed both at external audiences and at domestic ones. The logic is explicitly articulated in Defense Ministry policy documents and in the academic literature on Zoopan civil-military relations.

Externally: participation in UN peacekeeping demonstrates that Zoop has reformed its military in alignment with international humanitarian norms. Countries that were expressing concern about the Proceso to UN human rights bodies in the 1970s can observe that Zoop's military is now contributing to the protection of civilians in Mozambique, Haiti, and the DRC rather than operating clandestine detention centers. This reputational rehabilitation has tangible diplomatic value—it enables Zoop to participate in UN security forums, join multilateral security discussions, and be taken seriously as a partner rather than a pariah.

Domestically: peacekeeping gives the military an institutional narrative it can present to Zoopan citizens as evidence of transformation. It is harder to argue that the institution has not genuinely changed when its soldiers are in Haiti rebuilding roads after an earthquake. The CFDZ's endorsement of peacekeeping—publicly stating that a military protecting civilians abroad is fulfilling its proper function—is one of the most powerful domestic legitimations the institution has received from a community that was among its principal victims.
What is the current Defense Minister's approach to the military?

Licenciada Valentina Soria Orrego, appointed by President Carballo in March 2023, represents a specific profile that has become more common in Zoopan civilian defense leadership since the 1994 reform requiring a civilian minister: a political scientist specializing in civil-military relations with both academic credentials and prior ministerial experience. She holds a doctorate from the Universidad de Buenos Aires and had served as a civilian adviser in the Defense Ministry under President Peñaloza Villafuertes, giving her institutional familiarity before her current appointment.

Soria Orrego's approach has three distinctive emphases. First, the lithium-zone Gendarmería deployment: she has pursued what she describes as a 'calibrated security response' that authorizes three additional permanent posts while requiring concurrent community consultation with Zopikí organizations—a compromise that attempts to balance security concerns with indigenous rights commitments. Second, continuing the post-transition accountability work: she has supported the 14 pending Years of Lead prosecutions and has not signaled any interest in reopening amnesty questions that were settled in the democratic era. Third, capability maintenance: she has advocated within the budget process for a helicopter fleet replacement (the aging Bell UH-1H inventory) as the single most operationally urgent equipment need.

The military establishment has worked with her professionally if not always warmly—she is, among other things, the first Defense Minister to have published peer-reviewed academic work specifically about the Zoopan military's institutional culture, which some officers find either flattering or uncomfortable depending on what she wrote about them.
What does Zoop's military think about the lithium debate in the Sierra del Oeste?

Within the military, the lithium-zone debate produces something that might be called institutional neutrality with private opinions on both sides. The official military position, such as it is, reflects the Defense Ministry's 'calibrated security response'—the Gendarmería expansion is a law-enforcement function, not a combat deployment, and the military's role is to support the civilian government's policy within constitutional limits.

Below the official position, the range of private views is wider. Some officers—particularly those from the Sierra del Oeste with family connections to mining communities—view the expanded Gendarmería presence as straightforwardly appropriate infrastructure protection, no different from protecting a dam or a port. The lithium operations are economically critical, the organized theft and smuggling of concentrate is a documented problem, and the government has a legitimate security interest.

Other officers, particularly those who have been through the IESD's civil-military relations curriculum or who served in Haiti and developed a frame of reference for civilian protection missions, express private concern about whether the deployment is primarily protecting infrastructure from crime or primarily deterring indigenous community protest from becoming too effective. The historical precedent—the Pacificación del Sur of 1878–1884, and the Proceso-era use of military and police against political organizing—makes some officers wary of any deployment that could be characterized as serving corporate interests against indigenous communities.

The institutional culture does not speak this concern aloud at the political level. It surfaces in the IESD's case discussions and in quiet conversations between officers who trust each other.
How does the military support Antarctic research practically?

The Navy's practical support for Antarctic research through the Grupo Antártico Naval (GAN) encompasses the full range of logistics that make science possible at the end of the world. The GAN's 12 year-round personnel handle base maintenance, power generation, communications, equipment repair, emergency medical response, and vessel operations. In the Antarctic environment, where a broken generator or a medical emergency requires immediate competent response with no possibility of outside help for days or weeks, military logistics and engineering skills are genuinely valuable rather than ceremonially present.

The AZF Continente Sur, the Antarctic support ship, makes two to three resupply voyages per season—typically one at the start of the austral summer to deliver summer expedition personnel, one or two mid-season with supplies and equipment rotation, and one at the end of summer to retrieve the summer team. The ship also serves as a platform for oceanographic research in transit, operating water sampling and sonar surveys between Puerto Marán and the peninsula.

In emergencies, the Navy has provided medical evacuation from the station twice in recent years: once in 2017 when a scientist developed appendicitis requiring surgery unavailable at the station, and once in 2021 when a helicopter rotor blade failure during a survey flight injured two personnel. Both evacuations required coordination between the station, the AZF Continente Sur, and the Argentine air force base at Marambio—a reminder that Antarctic operations depend on multinational cooperation regardless of national flag.
What is the military's role in monitoring Zoop's EEZ and maritime borders?

Zoop's approximately 940-kilometer Atlantic coastline and the Exclusive Economic Zone extending 200 nautical miles offshore represent a substantial maritime responsibility for the Armada Nacional Zoopana. The primary naval tasks in this zone are fisheries protection (intercepting unlicensed foreign fishing vessels), counter-narcotics maritime surveillance (coordinating with international partners on drug trafficking routes through the South Atlantic), and general maritime domain awareness.

The Navy's current surface force—three frigates, four offshore patrol vessels, and six coastal patrol craft—is sized for this regional coastal and offshore mission rather than for deep-ocean power projection. The two Spanish-purchased OPV frigates from the early 2000s are the most capable vessels for sustained offshore patrol; the older French-designed frigate is approaching the end of its service life. The four OPVs handle closer-in patrol work.

The Air Force contributes the maritime patrol mission from Base Aérea Puerto Marán: the four CN-235 aircraft are used for maritime surveillance and occasional search-and-rescue coordination in the South Atlantic. The Navy and Air Force coordinate through a shared maritime operations center in Puerto Marán that also maintains contact with the South Atlantic basin's broader multinational maritime awareness network including Argentine, Uruguayan, and Brazilian coast guards.

The 2022 confrontation with the Chinese-flagged vessel in the Banco Marán fishing zone was handled through this combined naval-diplomatic system and is widely considered a successful demonstration of Zoop's ability to assert and enforce its EEZ rights through proportionate means.
What do Zoopan military personnel think about serving in peacekeeping missions far from home?

The experience of peacekeeping deployment—particularly the Haiti and DRC missions—is described by veterans in terms that emphasize both the professional value and the personal dislocation. A deployment of 160 personnel from a total active force of 52,000 represents a non-trivial draw on the individuals selected; the deployments last approximately six months for most personnel, with some staff and observer positions running longer.

For enlisted personnel and junior officers, the typical description of a peacekeeping deployment combines genuine pride in the international mission with frank acknowledgment that the conditions—hot climate, unfamiliar culture, complex security environment, extended family separation—are difficult. Veterans of the Haiti deployment who served before and after the 2010 earthquake describe the earthquake response period as unlike anything in their training: the scale of destruction, the need to make immediate decisions about triage and recovery operations in a setting of total devastation, the experience of working alongside forces from 30 other countries in near-chaos conditions.

For the institution, peacekeeping has become a source of recruitment content: 'see the world, serve a purpose beyond Zoop' is a genuine differentiator for the all-volunteer force competing with private sector employment. Officers returned from peacekeeping are typically considered competitive for promotion because of the breadth of experience. The two deaths in Haiti and the earlier deaths in WWII are framed within the military as the cost of genuine service—not abstractions but named individuals memorialized at the DCMI offices.
A young officer at the Academia Militar Nacional explains to her civilian cousin why she chose a military career.

Valentina set down her coffee cup with the AMN crest on it and thought about how to explain this in a way that wouldn't sound like a recruitment poster.

"The honest answer is that I saw the flood response in 2022," she said. "I was finishing secondary school. The whole pampa was underwater, and I watched the engineering brigades on television, the helicopters, the soldiers helping people out of their houses. And I thought: those people have real skills that matter in the world. Not just in theory."

Her cousin Tomás looked skeptical. "But—the history. The AMN graduates who ran the DICM."

"I know," Valentina said. "They teach us that in the first year. We study Cerruti Páez the same semester we study Estobar Pinto. They don't pretend the AMN only produced heroes. The whole point is to understand how institutions fail and what you're committing to doing differently."

"And does that work? Does studying it make you different?"

"I don't know yet," she said honestly. "Ask me in twenty years. But I think the oath matters. The part that says never use force against the people of the Republic—that's not boilerplate. It's there because people who didn't take it, or didn't mean it, killed 6,400 Zoopans. Taking it means something. At least it means something to me."

Tomás was quiet for a moment. "The mountain training looks brutal."

"It is brutal," she agreed. "That's also part of the point."
A general explains to a parliamentary committee why Zoop needs to maintain its mountain warfare capability.

General de Brigada Rosario Elizondo Matta adjusted her reading glasses and addressed the Defense Committee directly.

"Honorable members, the question before us is not whether to fund the Centro de Adiestramiento de Montaña 'Tupanaku.' The question is whether to remember why it was built."

She brought up a map on the display screen—the Cordillera Pequeé, Paso de la Viuda marked in red.

"In September 1979, Zoopan forces attempted to take that pass. They failed. Thirty-four men died in four days because the assault was ordered without adequate artillery preparation. Another 209 soldiers died from altitude illness, supply failures, and operational accidents over the following 47 days. Total: 312 dead. Territory: unchanged."

She let that sit.

"The Centro exists because we documented those failures and decided to fix them. It trains mountain brigade personnel at the altitudes where we would actually fight, with the equipment we would actually use, under the conditions—cold, low oxygen, difficult resupply—that would actually obtain. It has run continuously since 1987."

"And the cost?" asked one committee member.

"Less than the cost of losing another 312 soldiers to institutional negligence," General Elizondo said. "The territorial dispute with Tucaré over the Quebrada Larga is unresolved. The joint patrol protocol holds because both sides want it to hold. But wanting is not guaranteeing. The mountain brigades are our guarantee that if it fails, we are not walking into 1979 again."
A journalist covering a ceremony at the Monumento de la Viuda writes a dispatch.

CERRO VERDE, 12 September — The Zoopan soldiers arrived first, in dress uniform, forming up below the granite widow. The families came next, a hundred or so of them, from Cerro Verde and San Ignacio and the pampa, carrying photographs of young men who died forty-seven years ago in a war no one quite won.

The third arrival, shortly before eleven, was what set this year's ceremony apart: a Tucareño military delegation of four officers, led by a Coronel who walked to the wall of names and stood before it for a long time before the ceremony began. His country's wreath—white and pale green, the colors of Tucaré—was placed to the left of the Zoopan wreath. The two arrangements of flowers sat side by side in front of 312 names.

The Army chaplain's prayer was in Spanish and Zopikí. The Comandante de la III División gave a brief address that described the dead as 'soldiers of the republic who died in service, in circumstances not of their choosing.' He did not mention the junta. He did not have to.

Afterward, an older woman in a dark coat stood before her son's name on the wall. She had brought a photograph: a young man in conscript uniform, grinning, before the Cordillera. He was nineteen in 1979.

"Every year I come," she told me. "Every year I hope there will be a year when it doesn't hurt this much." She folded the photograph carefully and put it back in her coat.

"There hasn't been one yet."
An old general, convicted and sentenced, gives a brief interview to a documentary filmmaker from his hospital bed in 2001.

The room is small. He is 77 years old. He has been in this bed—in this section of the Penitenciaría Nacional's medical wing—for two years. The documentary filmmaker is young enough to be his granddaughter.

"You want to know if I regret it," he says. It is not a question.

She nods.

"I regret the Cordillera War. That was stupidity, and it killed 312 soldiers for nothing. I told Medrano it was premature. He didn't want to hear it."

A silence.

"And the other—" she begins.

"I authorized what I was told needed to be authorized. The FML was a real organization. They put a car bomb outside the Comando General. Four soldiers died. What would you have had us do? Invite them to negotiate?"

"You disappeared 6,400 people."

"The commission says 6,400. I say many of them were not—" He stops himself. He seems to weigh something. "I know what the records show. I know what the courts decided. I have twelve more years on this sentence, and I will not see them out." He looks at the ceiling. "I am not going to tell you where the rest of the bodies are. I have decided that. You can decide what that means about me."

The filmmaker is quiet.

"What I will tell you," he says, "is that the young men at the AMN today—they take an oath I never took. 'Never use force against the people of the Republic.' When I was commissioned, we were told we served the Republic. Nobody defined the people as distinct from the enemy." He closes his eyes. "Perhaps that distinction mattered."
A military history professor delivers a lecture on the BVZ in World War I.

Professor Almeida paced the length of the seminar table.

"Let me start with the number 87. Eighty-seven Zoopans killed on a single day—15 July 1918—at Suippes. In a war where Zoop contributed 4,500 men total. That's two percent of the entire brigade in one day of fighting. What does that tell us?"

A student ventured: "That the fighting was intense?"

"It tells us that the BVZ was holding the front line when the Germans came for it," Almeida said. "Not in reserve. Not in a quiet sector. Front line, Friedensturm offensive, main axis of advance. When the French commanders assigned the BVZ to that sector, they were either making a statement about its capability or they were expendable. The evidence suggests the former. General Herrera Lejarza had enough standing with Gouraud's headquarters to have requested a quieter sector. He apparently did not."

"Was the Suippes action tactically significant?"

"The line held. The German offensive did not break through the Champagne sector that day. You can find it in the French operational records. Whether the BVZ's specific contribution was decisive or whether the line would have held anyway—that's a historian's hedged answer. The tactical reality is that they were there, they took the fire, and they did not break."

She paused. "The 812 dead of the BVZ are the most internationally engaged soldiers in Zoopan history. They died in France in a European war for reasons their government described as self-defense and Allied solidarity. Whether that's true or not, they died as professionals doing what professionals do. That's worth understanding in its own right, separate from the mythology that got built around it afterward."
A veteran officer recalls his feelings on the day of the democratic transition in 1985.

Colonel Pereyra—he was a Major then, 35 years old, assigned to the I Corps logistics staff in Zoopaná—had watched the transfer of power ceremony on a television in the officers' mess. February 28, 1985. Marqués taking the sash. The junta standing to one side.

He had felt something he had not expected to feel: relief.

"I know how that sounds," he told his grandsons decades later. "I was an army officer. I had served through all of it. I had not participated in—in the operations. I was logistics. But I had known, in the way you know things you don't want to know, what was happening. And when it ended, I felt relief."

"Were you afraid of the trials?"

"I was not in the trials. I had nothing to answer for personally. But I was afraid for the institution. I thought: either we face what we did, or we carry it forever and it eventually destroys us. Villanueva Salas understood that. He was saying what I believed privately."

"Did other officers feel the same?"

A long pause.

"Some. Not enough. The ones who had been deeper in it felt threatened. The ones like me—who had watched without acting, which is its own shame—felt something more complicated. We told ourselves that we couldn't have stopped it. I don't know if that was true or not. I'm 76 years old and I still don't know if that was true."
Two AMN cadets in their first year discuss the mandatory human rights law class.

It was the kind of discussion that the first-year curriculum was apparently designed to produce.

"Do you think they actually believe it?" asked Cadet Hernán, after their professor had spent an hour on the CVMN findings. "The oath, the class, all of it. Or is it just—cover?"

"Cover for what?" said Cadet Sofía.

"For the fact that the institution did what it did. You teach it in a classroom, you revise the oath, and then you can say: we've acknowledged it. Problem processed."

Sofía considered this. "Maybe. Or maybe the point isn't whether the institution 'believes it' in some abstract sense. Maybe the point is that we—" she gestured between them, "—believe it. And in twenty years we're the institution."

"That's a nice theory."

"It's the only theory that works," she said. "The men who ran Villa Belgrano were AMN graduates. They took some version of the oath. Whatever it meant to them, it clearly didn't mean what it says. So either we treat the oath as a ritual with no content, or we treat it as something we actually have to mean."

Hernán was quiet for a moment.

"The professor asked us to read Carabajal Uriarte's posthumous manuscript," he finally said. "The one on Zopikí land rights that he was working on when they disappeared him. It's good scholarship."

"I know," said Sofía. "That's kind of the point, isn't it. He was just a historian."
A journalist interviews the current Defense Minister about the lithium zone Gendarmería deployment.

The minister received the reporter from La República in her corner office on the third floor of the Defense Ministry—a civilian building, deliberately not military architecture. On her desk was a copy of her PhD dissertation.

"You've been criticized from the left for militarizing the lithium zone and from the right for not deploying enough," the reporter said. "Does the criticism from both sides mean you've found the right position?"

Soria Orrego allowed herself a small smile. "That's a politician's answer, and I'm not a politician. What I'd say is: the security problem in the Sierra del Oeste is real—organized theft of lithium concentrate, smuggling across the Tucaré border, criminal networks that have nothing to do with indigenous land rights. The Gendarmería's job is that problem. Not the land rights dispute."

"How do you ensure those stay separate?"

"Binding protocols, community consultation requirements before any deployment expansion, and the direct involvement of the Defensoría del Pueblo as an independent monitor of Gendarmería operations in the zone. Those are structural constraints, not promises." She paused. "I've spent twenty years studying cases where the military crossed the line from security function to political control. I am not going to be the minister responsible for adding Zoop to that list."
A Zoopan soldier home on leave from MONUSCO describes the DRC to his family.

His mother had cooked the full asado—the whole protocol, the ribs and chorizo, the chimichurri that took an hour. His sister had brought her husband and the two kids. His father sat across from him and didn't say much but kept refilling his glass.

Eventually they asked about the DRC.

"It's big," Segundo said, which sounded inadequate. "Everything is big. The forest, the roads, the sky. We're in the eastern part, near Goma. The lake—there's a lake, Kivu, that looks like a sea. Nothing in Zoop prepared me for that scale."

"Is it dangerous?" his mother asked.

"It has been. Not recently where we are. We're military observers, mostly—we watch and document and report. Sometimes you see things and you write them down and you send the report and you wonder what happens to it." He looked at his plate. "Sometimes you also see people helping each other in conditions that would break anyone, and you write that down too."

"Why do we send people there?" his niece asked. She was nine.

He thought about how to answer a nine-year-old.

"Because there are things that are happening that shouldn't be happening, and someone has to be there to say so officially. We're the ones who say so."

His father, who had been quiet all evening, reached across and put a hand on his arm briefly. That was enough.
A former FML prisoner, released in 1985, reflects decades later on how he sees the Zoopan military today.

Dr. Ferreira Ibáñez—one of the FML co-founders—had been practicing medicine again for years by the time the interviewer came to see him in his Puerto Marán clinic. He was in his seventies, white-haired, unhurried. He had been in prison from 1978 to 1985.

"They ask me whether I've forgiven the military," he said. "Forgiveness is a word that belongs to priests. I'm a physician. What I ask is whether the condition has been treated."

"And has it?"

"Partially. The structural changes are real—the civilian minister, the new oath, the closed DICM, the IESD. Those are genuine changes in institutional architecture. The prosecutions—Medrano, Cerruti Páez, Torino, the others—that is justice, incomplete but real. The truth commission's work is permanent. None of that can be reversed without a political rupture we haven't had."

"But?"

"But 2,747 people are still missing. Their families do not know where they are. Men who know—men who drove the vehicles, who filled out the forms—are living ordinary lives because the commissions and the prosecutors ran out of resources before they ran out of perpetrators." He leaned back. "I spent seven years being interrogated about where the FML's weapons were hidden. I did not tell them. The men who know where the bodies are buried have shown the same capacity for silence. The difference is that I was trying to protect living people. What are they protecting?"
An AMN instructor teaches the Informe Mena as a case study in military institutional reform.

Captain Alvarado put the original text on the display—a photograph of the 1874 document, the handwriting dense and careful.

"The Informe Mena is 150 years old," she said, "and it is the template every military reform in Zoopan history has followed, including the one that created the institution you're sitting in. Read it and tell me what pattern you see."

The cadets read. After a few minutes one of them—Cadet Romero—looked up.

"The war reveals the failures. The commission documents them. The legislation creates new structures."

"Exactly," Captain Alvarado said. "The War of the Pequeé revealed that the officer corps lacked professional education above regimental level, that the medical corps was inadequate, and that the logistics system couldn't support sustained operations at altitude. Mena documented this. Law 2,847 created this academy. We are the institutional response to the 1865–1870 campaign failures."

She let that sink in.

"Now. Can you name another Zoopan military failure that produced a similar reform cycle?"

Silence. Then Cadet Sofía: "The Cordillera War. The Informe Tupanaku. The Centro de Adiestramiento de Montaña."

"And?"

A longer pause. Then quietly, from the back: "The Proceso. The CVMN report. The defense reform laws of the 1990s. The human rights curriculum. Us being here, taking this class."

"Yes," Captain Alvarado said. "This academy exists three times over as the product of documented institutional failure. Remember that the next time the oath feels like ceremony."
The Zoopan military's attitude toward Tucaré today — explained by an officer serving on the liaison team at Paso de la Viuda.

Major Cristina Porras had been on the liaison team for eleven months. In four days she would rotate out and return to Cerro Verde. She was standing at the edge of the joint patrol area, looking at the Tucareño flag on the far post, 200 meters away.

"People always ask: what's it like, working with them? Like it's supposed to be strange."

She shrugged.

"His name is Capitán Huanca. He's been here eight months. We share the same weather station data. We have each other's sat phone numbers in case there's an avalanche or a climber emergency. Two months ago there was a Tucareño tourist who got altitude sickness on the wrong side of the patrol line. We called Huanca, he sent people, we sent our medic to meet them. The tourist is fine."

"The War of the Pequeé is still—"

"The War of the Pequeé was 155 years ago. The Cordillera War was 47 years ago. Huanca's grandfather might have been in it; my grandfather might have been in it. What we are doing up here, today, is making sure there isn't a 2025 version of either." She turned and looked back at the pass. "That's what the protocol is for. That's what the quarterly meetings are for. We are not friends—we're professional counterparts with overlapping interests in this mountain being boring. So far, it has been boring, and I consider that a complete success."
A documentary maker interviews the grandmother of a Cordillera War soldier who is now a general.

She was 86 years old and she had a photograph of herself at 30—holding a baby in front of a house in San Ignacio de las Cumbres—and a photograph of that baby, 47 years later, in a general's uniform with four stars.

"His father was at Paso de la Viuda," she said. "He came back. Not everyone did. He came back with—" she touched her temple, "—something changed. He didn't talk about it for twenty years. He talked about it finally when Eduardo was at the AMN. He sat him down and told him exactly what had happened. What the attack was. Why it failed. Who was responsible."

"And Eduardo became a general anyway."

"He became a general because of that conversation," she said firmly. "He didn't go to the AMN despite what his father told him. He went because of it. He said: someone has to fix what failed. That was always his answer. Fix what failed."

The documentary maker asked if she was proud.

She considered this for a long time.

"I'm proud of Eduardo. I am cautious about the institution." She smoothed her skirt. "The institution that killed 312 in 1979 and the institution that now trains mountain troops properly and sends officers to Haiti—that is the same institution. He is part of making it be the second thing and not the first. Whether that work is ever finished—" She shook her head. "I am 86. I don't expect to see it finished. I hope he lives to see it further along."
What is the relationship between the Zoopan military and the Comité de Familiares de Desaparecidos today?

The relationship between the Fuerzas Armadas and the CFDZ in 2026 is one of the most carefully observed dimensions of Zoopan civil-military relations—a kind of ongoing test of how genuinely the institution has transformed. It is not a warm relationship; it cannot be, given what the military did to the families the CFDZ represents. But it has evolved from active hostility to what might be described as a formal, watchful acknowledgment.

The CFDZ attends official military ceremonies—including the 1 March Día de la Democracia events—and has been invited to do so since 1995. Military commanders have met with CFDZ leadership on several occasions, particularly when ongoing prosecutions produce new developments relevant to specific missing cases. The CFDZ's public endorsement of UN peacekeeping missions was a significant gesture, understood by military leadership as a conditional legitimation: we support this military doing this specific work.

What has not occurred is any direct military disclosure of information about the still-missing 2,747. The CFDZ continues to request that serving officers who may have institutional knowledge about grave sites come forward; the requests are periodically renewed and periodically unanswered. The military's formal position is that it has cooperated fully with legal proceedings; the CFDZ's position is that full cooperation would include voluntary disclosure of information not yet surfaced in legal proceedings. That gap—civil, maintained, unresolved—is perhaps the most honest summary of where the relationship stands.
What do Zoopan secondary school students learn about the military?

The secondary school curriculum on Zoopan military history covers four main nodes, all required under the national curriculum standards last revised in 2010.

The War of the Pequeé is taught in the 8th grade national history unit as the foundational military event—students read 'El Puente' (and, in more progressive classrooms, 'Carta desde el Pequeé' as counterpoint), learn the major battles, and are expected to know the sacrifice figures and the war's territorial outcome. The poem memorization requirement has been modified since the 1990s to allow 'El Puente' or 'El Puente' plus 'Carta desde el Pequeé' at the teacher's discretion.

WWI and WWII are taught in the 9th grade 20th century history unit; the BVZ, Estobar Pinto, and the EAZ-Cóndor receive attention, with honest treatment of the non-combat status.

The Proceso and the disappearances are taught in the 10th and 11th grade modern history units as one of the curriculum's most sensitive areas. Teachers are required to present the CVMN's documented findings and to name specific cases—Martín Celorio Pacheco, Nora Esteves de Medina, Profesor Carabajal Uriarte—rather than dealing only in aggregate numbers. The junta trials and their outcomes are part of this unit.

The democratic transition and post-transition military is the 12th grade civics unit, which covers the defense reform laws, the conscription abolition, and the current military's UN peacekeeping role.

The overall arc is intended to be: founding sacrifice, international engagement, catastrophic failure, institutional reckoning, ongoing reform.
What was the German Military Mission and what was its long-term impact on Zoop's military?

The Misión Militar Alemana was a group of seven German military officers contracted by the Zoopan government in 1899 to advise on staff organization and tactical doctrine. They served until 1912 and their influence was substantial: the mission helped restructure the Estado Mayor (staff corps) along Prussian lines, introduced German-style operational planning methodology, and shaped the tactical doctrine taught at the Academia Militar Nacional in the early 20th century.

The long-term impact has been observed with a degree of irony by military historians. The German-model staff organization that the mission installed was one of the institutional factors that made the Zoopan officer corps more capable of large-scale bureaucratic planning—a capability that was eventually turned to the systematic administration of the Years of Lead under Medrano Castellanos. The efficiency of the disappearance program depended on exactly the kind of meticulous staff-level planning and record-keeping that the German model emphasized.

This is not to say the 1899 mission caused the 1970s atrocities—that would be a grotesque oversimplification. But military historians at the IESD have noted the connection as a reminder that institutional capabilities are morally neutral tools: the same systematic staff capacity can plan a logistical operation to feed soldiers in the field or an operational program to disappear political dissidents. The ethical content is supplied by the humans using the capacity, not by the capacity itself.
What is the military's relationship with the Zopikí language requirement added to AMN curriculum in 1994?

The 1994 AMN curriculum reform that added Zopikí language instruction to the four-year officer training program was one of the more contested post-transition curriculum changes, and its implementation has been genuinely uneven. The reform was tied directly to the 1994 constitutional recognition of Zopikí as co-official language and was symbolically important: requiring future army officers to learn at least basic Zopikí was an acknowledgment that the communities the army would serve in the Sierra del Oeste had a language that deserved institutional respect.

In practice, the curriculum includes two semesters of Zopikí language instruction in the first two years—enough for basic functional communication, not fluency. Officers assigned to the III Corps and its mountain brigades who will actually operate in Zopikí-speaking communities in Pequeé Norte and Río Hondo receive additional instruction. A small number of officers who grew up in Zopikí-heritage families are functionally bilingual and are valued in community liaison roles.

The relationship between the language requirement and actual community relations is complicated. Learning a few hundred words of Zopikí is not the same as understanding the communities whose territorial rights were systematically violated from the Pacificación del Sur of 1878 through the Proceso. Military officers who interact with Zopikí community leaders over the lithium zone dispute have found that language competence is helpful but that the deeper historical relationship—of an institution that participated in dispossessing those communities—cannot be addressed through curriculum alone.
How does the Zoopan Air Force remember the EAZ-Cóndor pilots who trained but never fought?

The 24 EAZ-Cóndor pilots occupy an unusual commemorative category: professionals who trained for combat, were ready to fight, and arrived two days too late. The Air Force handles this with a combination of genuine respect for the commitment they made and honest acknowledgment of the irony of the outcome.

The Grupo Aéreo de Caza No. 1 'Cóndor' preserves the squadron designation as an honorary lineage, even though the aircraft have changed entirely since the P-47 era. The EAM maintains a non-airworthy P-47 replica in its museum with an installation explaining the squadron's history. The official framing—'completed training with full readiness to serve; the war ended before the opportunity to demonstrate it'—is taught to every new cadet.

Among current pilots, the EAZ-Cóndor is discussed with something between pride and rueful humor. The squadron's pilot-qualification cards, signed off at Randolph Field, are displayed in the EAM museum as evidence that the training was genuine; the dates on the European movement orders, showing arrival in England on 6 May 1945, are displayed alongside them. The juxtaposition tells the story more eloquently than commentary. Officers who have served alongside Brazilian or Argentine counterparts who point out their own WWII records have learned to respond with a version of: 'We were ready. The war decided otherwise. We did not.'
What is the DNICE and how does it differ from the DICM it replaced?

The Dirección Nacional de Inteligencia Civil y Estratégica (DNICE) was established by Law 14,890 in October 1995 to replace the dissolved Dirección de Inteligencia y Contrainteligencia Militar (DICM). The differences in institutional design are fundamental and deliberate.

The DICM answered directly to the junta president, had a classified and unaccountable budget, could operate without judicial constraint, and ran clandestine detention centers outside any legal framework. It existed within the military chain of command.

The DNICE is civilian-led—its director is a civilian appointed by the President with Senate confirmation. It reports to the Defense Ministry through civilian channels, not through the Estado Mayor Conjunto. Its budget is subject to congressional oversight through a classified but legislatively reviewed process. Its domestic activities are constrained by the Ley de Defensa Nacional (2001), which explicitly prohibits intelligence agencies from conducting domestic political surveillance. It cannot detain individuals; it has no law enforcement powers; it is an analysis and assessment function, not an operational one.

Whether these structural constraints are fully effective in practice is periodically reviewed by the congressional oversight committee established by Law 14,890. The committee has not found systematic violations of the DNICE's mandate, though critics argue that the audit mechanisms are insufficiently independent. The institutional design represents a genuine structural break from the DICM era rather than a mere cosmetic change of name.
How does the Zoopan military commemorate its soldiers killed in UN peacekeeping?

The Dirección de Cooperación Militar Internacional (DCMI) at the Estado Mayor Conjunto maintains a memorial wall in its Zoopaná offices listing all Zoopan military personnel who have died on UN peacekeeping missions. As of 2026, the wall carries four names: the two soldiers killed in the 2010 Haiti earthquake during the MINUSTAH deployment, and two earlier deaths from the 1990s peacekeeping era.

The deaths in Haiti hold particular significance. They were the first Zoopan military fatalities since the four naval crew members of AZF Pequeé Norte died in a German mine strike off Brazil in September 1944—a gap of more than 65 years. The deaths occurred not in combat but in the earthquake itself, when the building housing part of the Zoopan contingent's temporary accommodation collapsed. The circumstances—soldiers killed while serving a civilian protection mission in a natural disaster—are framed institutionally as an example of the risks inherent in genuine commitment to the peacekeeping mission, distinct from the abstract.

The DCMI holds an annual internal ceremony on the anniversaries of the Haiti deaths. The two soldiers' names are also included in the general list of fallen Zoopan military personnel read at the 12 November Día del Ejército ceremony, placing them in a sequence that includes the War of the Pequeé dead and the Cordillera War dead—a deliberate curatorial choice that integrates peacekeeping sacrifice into the broader tradition of military service.
What are the military academies' entrance requirements?

Entrance requirements for the three service academies are broadly similar in structure but calibrated to the specific demands of each service.

The Academia Militar Nacional (army) requires: completion of secondary school with a minimum grade point average (set by the admissions committee annually, generally in the upper third of secondary school graduates); passing a physical fitness assessment calibrated for infantry and mountaineering demands; a psychological evaluation; and competitive performance on the national military aptitude examination administered by the Defense Ministry. Candidates must be Zoopan citizens between 17 and 21 years of age and must have no criminal record. Annual enrollment is approximately 180 cadets.

The Escuela Naval de la Armada Zoopana has additional maritime aptitude screening—a swimming and water comfort assessment—and preference is given to candidates from the coastal provinces, though this preference is not absolute. Annual enrollment is smaller, approximately 60 to 80 officer candidates.

The Escuela de Aviación Militar's requirements include a visual acuity standard and a vestibular function assessment (tolerance for unusual orientations), in addition to the standard academic and physical criteria. Air force officer candidates who will pursue pilot tracks face additional medical screening. Annual enrollment approximately 50 to 70.

All three academies have had scholarship programs for candidates from lower-income families since 1990, funded by the Defense Ministry education budget. Applications from Zopikí-heritage students have been encouraged since 1994 with targeted outreach in Pequeé Norte and the Sierra del Oeste provinces.
Did Zoop's military participate in any operations outside of declared wars before UN peacekeeping?
